status_reasoning: Reviewers request clarification on viscosity measurements and drag force calculations (16-24 pN), questioning whether the observed viscosity is solely from the membrane or includes motor-microtubule interactions. They suggest the mode of failure (motor detachment vs. glycoprotein detachment) needs clarification and propose additional experiments to isolate membrane viscosity effects.

Reviewers find the colocalization of bead motility with IFT trains convincing, noting 'the pausing is abundantly clear and quite convincing in Video 2.' Their comments focus only on figure presentation improvements, not on the validity of the underlying data showing IFT trains carry FMG1-B cargo.

Reviewers accept that IFT trains pause through surface adhesion of FMG cargos, stating the pausing is 'abundantly clear and quite convincing in Video 2.' Their comments address only figure clarity issues, not the scientific validity of the pausing observations and their relationship to gliding motility.

Reviewers do not challenge the dynein-1b mutant experiments or ciliobrevin D data showing dynein-1b drives gliding motility. They accept the evidence that kinesin plays an inhibitory role, with comments focused only on presentation and clarification rather than questioning the experimental findings or conclusions.

Reviewers do not question the Ca2+-dependence findings showing that Ca2+ is required for IFT train pausing and FMG1-B attachment to trains. The data showing frequent pauses in Ca2+ presence and reduced pausing in Ca2+-deprived conditions are accepted without challenge.

Reviewers accept the optical trapping force measurements (20-30 pN) and the conclusion that at least four motors transport IFT trains. They request clarification on QPD signal interpretation in Figure 5B but do not challenge the force measurements or motor number estimates themselves.

Reviewers explicitly state that 'The data indicate that multiple motors attached to an IFT train may not be able to reach their maximum stall force: this statement is not well supported by the data.' This directly challenges the claim about motors not reaching maximum stall force.

Reviewers note that 'The caption to Figure 5 gives the incorrect impression that the typical method of reversal of the direction of gliding motility of a Chlamydomonas involves the lifting of one flagellum off the substrate,' stating that most reversals occur with both flagella in contact. This suggests the description of gliding direction control mechanisms needs correction.

Reviewers do not challenge the reciprocal motor coordination data showing that only one type of motor is active at a time and that motors do not engage in tug-of-war. The temperature-shift experiments with motor mutants are accepted without critique.

Reviewers accept the findings that viscous drag slows IFT trains carrying beads and that this explains the difference between gliding speed and IFT speed. Their questions about viscosity measurements (comment 1) relate to methodology clarification rather than challenging these observations.

Reviewers do not challenge the central conclusion that gliding motility is powered by IFT machinery along microtubules, with dynein motors pulling the cell when IFT trains are surface-tethered. The article was 'favorably evaluated' and this core mechanism is not questioned.
